paragraphs.heading: Handedness in molecules
paragraphs.text: A molecule or ion is chiral if it cannot be laid exactly over its mirror image, whatever rotations, shifts and some changes of shape you try. This property is called chirality. The word comes from the Ancient Greek for hand, the standard example of an object that behaves this way.

paragraphs.heading: Enantiomers
paragraphs.text: A chiral molecule exists in two mirror-image forms called enantiomers, often labelled right-handed or left-handed. The pair share the same chemical properties, except when they react with other chiral compounds. Their physical properties also match, except that they often show opposite optical activity. An equal mix of the two, called a racemic mixture, differs both chemically and physically from either pure form.

paragraphs.heading: Stereocenters
paragraphs.text: Chirality usually arises from a stereogenic element, and the most common one is a stereocenter. In organic compounds this is most often a carbon atom bonded to four different groups in a tetrahedral arrangement. Less often, atoms such as N, P, S and Si fill this role, provided they carry four distinct substituents, counting lone pair electrons. Each stereocenter has two possible configurations, called R and S.

paragraphs.heading: One center or many
paragraphs.text: An organic compound with just one stereogenic carbon is always chiral. With several, it usually is, but not always. If the centers are arranged so the molecule can take a shape with a plane of symmetry or an inversion point, it is achiral and is called a meso compound. Rarer kinds of chirality come from an axis, a plane or the curvature of the whole molecule; helicene, for instance, has helical chirality.

paragraphs.heading: Why biology cares
paragraphs.text: Most substances that matter in biology are chiral, including sugars, starch, cellulose, nucleic acids and all but one of the amino acids that build proteins. Living things typically contain just one of the two enantiomers of any given chiral compound. So organisms that consume such a compound can usually metabolize only one form. For the same reason, the two enantiomers of a drug can differ sharply in potency or effect.

paragraphs.heading: It depends on temperature
paragraphs.text: Whether a molecule counts as chiral can depend on how quickly its mirror-image shapes turn into each other. Butane has chiral twisted forms, but at room temperature rotation about its central C–C bond swaps them fast, so it is treated as achiral. If the temperature is low enough, that swapping slows and the molecule is then considered chiral. Molecules that stay chiral at room temperature because rotation about a single bond is restricted are said to show atropisomerism.
